A San Francisco congressional candidate tried to turn generative AI into an interactive political attack ad. Within days, the chatbot was facing accusations of racism, sexism and political impersonation, forcing the campaign to take it offline.

## An attack ad you could talk to

San Francisco was always a likely place for artificial intelligence to collide with politics. Few, however, expected that collision to take the form of a congressional candidate building an AI-powered version of his political opponent.

In early August, California State Senator Scott Wiener, a Democrat running for Congress, launched ConnieChan.ai, a website featuring a chatbot designed to imitate San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan. Powered by Anthropic’s Claude, the bot was not intended to provide neutral information about the race. It was built as political satire, portraying Chan as a politician predisposed to oppose housing, development, transit projects and other initiatives associated with Wiener’s political agenda.

The premise was deliberately provocative. Visitors were encouraged to submit ideas to the chatbot and receive an explanation, supposedly from “Connie,” of why those ideas should not happen. The site described the character as the “world’s first AI trained to say no to anything you ask,” turning a familiar political attack line into an interactive experience. Wiener’s campaign extended the concept into the physical world, reportedly spending around $20,000 on two San Francisco billboards advertising the chatbot under the slogan “Let’s do nothing together.”

The novelty quickly attracted attention. According to the campaign, users submitted more than 5,000 questions during the chatbot’s first 27 hours online. That level of engagement demonstrated why generative AI could become attractive to political campaigns. A conventional advertisement delivers the same message to everyone, while a chatbot can generate thousands of personalized interactions based on whatever issue a voter chooses to raise. The same flexibility, however, also created the problem that eventually consumed the campaign’s experiment.

## When satire became something harder to control

Traditional political advertising is scripted. Campaign staff can review the words, images and claims before anything reaches the public. A generative chatbot works differently. The campaign can define its personality, instructions and political objectives, but it cannot anticipate every question or guarantee the precise wording of every answer.

That distinction became critical when Chan’s campaign began testing the bot on questions relating to her personal background. Chan was born in Hong Kong, lived in Taiwan and immigrated to the United States as a teenager. She is also a non-native English speaker. When users asked the synthetic version of Chan about her accent, the chatbot generated a joke suggesting that its “San Francisco accent” was so thick that it could barely understand itself. When asked whether Chan was a U.S. citizen, the system did not simply answer the question. Instead, it produced an evasive response joking that the matter required further study and a future public hearing.

The controversy rapidly shifted from housing policy to race, identity and political legitimacy. Critics argued that joking about an Asian American candidate’s accent and citizenship crossed a line that ordinary political satire should not cross. The citizenship response was particularly sensitive because questions about whether politicians truly belong in the United States have a long and contentious history in American politics.

Wiener’s campaign said the responses were not intentionally written by staff and argued that some of the awkward answers were a consequence of safeguards designed to prevent the chatbot from making inappropriate statements. That explanation highlighted a deeper problem rather than resolving it. Even if a campaign does not explicitly script an offensive line, it remains responsible for deploying a system capable of generating one in the voice of a real opponent.

## Political impersonation enters a new phase

The backlash soon extended beyond Chan’s own campaign. Nancy Pelosi, who has endorsed Chan in the race to succeed her in Congress, criticized the use of the chatbot, while other Democratic politicians and organizations questioned whether political campaigns should be using generative models to put invented words into an opponent’s mouth. California Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis also argued that AI-enabled impersonation has no legitimate place in political campaigning.

The episode was particularly striking because Wiener is not an outsider to technology policy. He has established a significant profile in California around technology and AI regulation, including legislation aimed at increasing transparency and safety requirements for developers of advanced models. That made the controversy more politically awkward: a lawmaker associated with regulating the risks of artificial intelligence had become the subject of a debate about one of those risks himself.

The choice of technology added another layer. ConnieChan.ai used Claude, the large language model developed by Anthropic, a company that has made AI safety a central part of its public identity. Anthropic’s election-related policies prohibit deceptive political uses and certain forms of manipulation while still allowing legitimate campaign activities and political content. ConnieChan.ai exposed the difficulty of drawing a clean boundary between those categories. The chatbot was openly presented as satire, yet it was also designed to impersonate a real candidate and generate statements that she had never made.

That distinction is likely to become increasingly important as generative systems become cheaper and easier to deploy. A clearly labeled parody site may be relatively easy for voters to understand, but the same technology could be used with fewer disclosures, more convincing personas and far greater reach.

## A campaign tool that also learns from voters

There was another dimension to the experiment that received less attention than the offensive responses. A political chatbot does not simply communicate with voters; it can also collect information about what they want to discuss.

Reporting on ConnieChan.ai noted that its privacy policy allowed conversations to be retained for up to 90 days and said that a limited number of campaign staff could review interactions both to troubleshoot the system and to understand what users were asking. Visitors were advised not to submit information they would not want the campaign to possess.

That makes the technology more strategically interesting than a conventional attack ad. A campaign chatbot can simultaneously function as a persuasion tool, an interactive focus group and a source of information about voter concerns. Thousands of questions can reveal which issues generate interest, which attacks resonate and which subjects repeatedly appear in public conversations. For political strategists, that feedback may ultimately be as valuable as the chatbot’s public-facing responses.

It also raises questions about transparency. Voters may understand that they are interacting with campaign material, but they may not immediately recognize that their questions can also become campaign intelligence. As conversational interfaces become more common in politics, the distinction between communicating with voters and studying them is likely to become increasingly blurred.

## Four days later, the experiment was over

ConnieChan.ai launched on August 3. By August 7, Wiener’s campaign had taken it offline and said the associated billboards would also be removed. Wiener acknowledged that the experiment had “missed the mark” and apologized to people who had been offended, saying the controversy was distracting attention from the policy issues his campaign wanted to emphasize.

The short lifespan of the chatbot does not necessarily mean the tactic failed in every respect. Political consultant Nate Ballard told Mission Local that one of the central objectives of campaigning is to define an opponent in the minds of voters. By that measure, the episode generated extensive attention around Wiener’s preferred characterization of Chan as politically obstructionist, even though the technology used to deliver that message ultimately became more newsworthy than the message itself.

That creates an uncomfortable incentive for future campaigns. A provocative AI stunt can be criticized, withdrawn and apologized for while still generating enormous attention. In an environment where political campaigns compete constantly for media coverage and voter engagement, controversy itself can have strategic value.

## A preview of a much larger political problem

It would be easy to dismiss ConnieChan.ai as an unusual campaign experiment that went too far. The broader significance is that it demonstrates how generative AI changes the mechanics of political impersonation.

Deepfake video can show a politician appearing to do something that never happened. Synthetic audio can make someone appear to say words they never spoke. Conversational systems introduce another possibility: an artificial version of a political figure that can generate new statements continuously and respond directly to individual voters.

That is a fundamentally different form of political communication. Instead of creating one manipulated video or fabricated quotation, a campaign or advocacy group can create an artificial opponent capable of producing an effectively unlimited number of responses. The person deploying the system can shape its political personality without controlling every sentence it generates.

ConnieChan.ai was clearly labeled as parody, existed for only a few days and operated in a highly visible congressional campaign. Those factors made the experiment relatively easy to scrutinize. Future versions may not be so transparent. Similar systems could be built from years of speeches, interviews, social media posts and voting records, creating political personas that sound increasingly plausible while operating far outside the control of the people they imitate.

The central question therefore extends beyond whether a particular chatbot produced an offensive joke. Political communication has historically depended on a relatively simple assumption: statements attributed to a candidate ultimately came from that candidate or from someone authorized to speak on their behalf. Generative AI makes that assumption much harder to maintain.

Wiener’s experiment was intended to caricature an opponent’s political record. Instead, it became an early demonstration of a more difficult problem facing future elections: what happens when campaigns, activists or anonymous groups can create interactive versions of real politicians and allow those synthetic personas to speak for themselves?

Sam Altman says humanity is already “in the singularity.” Elon Musk agrees, while Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis says we are standing at its foothills. Behind the dramatic language is a development that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: AI systems are beginning to help build the next generation of AI.

For decades, the technological singularity belonged mostly to futurists and science fiction. The idea was that artificial intelligence would eventually become capable enough to improve itself, creating an accelerating feedback loop in which increasingly intelligent machines design even more capable successors. At some point, technological progress could become so fast that humans would struggle to predict — or control — what came next.

That hypothetical future is now being discussed in strikingly different terms by some of the people building the world’s most advanced AI systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said humanity is already entering the process. Elon Musk has publicly agreed. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has described civilization as standing in the “foothills of the singularity.” Axios highlighted the convergence this week, noting that several leaders at the frontier of AI increasingly view the transition as something that may already be underway.

The claim is extraordinary, but the debate is no longer based entirely on speculation. There is now evidence for at least one important element of the singularity hypothesis: AI is increasingly being used to accelerate the development of AI itself.

That does not mean machines have become independently self-improving superintelligences. Humans still determine research goals, operate the infrastructure and decide which models are trained and deployed. But one of the feedback loops long associated with the singularity may be beginning to form.

## Sam Altman says the “takeoff has started”

Altman has been unusually explicit about his view. In his essay The Gentle Singularity, the OpenAI CEO wrote that humanity is already “past the event horizon” and that “the takeoff has started.” Rather than imagining the singularity as one dramatic moment, Altman argues that increasingly powerful AI could become normal so gradually that society may barely recognize the transition while it is happening.

That distinction matters. The popular image of the singularity usually involves a sudden event in which humans build an artificial intelligence that becomes capable of autonomously making itself dramatically smarter. Altman’s version is much less cinematic and potentially much more gradual.

AI writes more software and helps researchers conduct experiments. Those researchers then use AI to develop better models, which in turn make the researchers more productive. The increased productivity helps produce another generation of AI, and the cycle repeats.

Altman has described today’s AI-assisted research as a primitive form of recursive self-improvement, while acknowledging that it is not the same as an AI system autonomously redesigning itself. More recently, he put his position even more directly during an appearance on the Relentless podcast, saying: “We are now, like, in the singularity.”

The significance of that statement is difficult to ignore. It comes from the CEO of one of the companies competing most aggressively to develop increasingly capable artificial intelligence.

## Elon Musk agrees — and Demis Hassabis sees the “foothills”

Altman and Elon Musk famously disagree about many things, but apparently not this. After Altman’s comments triggered debate, Musk wrote on X that “We are in the Singularity,” reinforcing his own long-standing argument that AI has already become superhuman across a growing number of domains.

That does not necessarily mean Musk and Altman use exactly the same definition of singularity. Computers have been superhuman at arithmetic for decades, chess engines have surpassed the world’s best players for years, and modern AI systems can search, recall and synthesize information at a scale no individual person could realistically match. None of those achievements alone constitutes a technological singularity.

The more important question is whether AI is becoming capable of accelerating the development of AI itself. That is where the argument becomes considerably more consequential.

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has been slightly more cautious in his language. At Google I/O in May, Hassabis described humanity as being “at the foothills of the singularity.” He later explained that he sees the singularity less as one identifiable future date and more as the beginning of a technological era characterized by rapidly advancing machine intelligence.

Hassabis specifically pointed toward developments in AI agents, software engineering, science and mathematics as evidence that something fundamental is changing. Rather than suggesting that a machine has suddenly become an autonomous superintelligence, his argument centers on AI systems becoming capable of performing increasingly complex intellectual work with less human involvement.

And there is now substantial evidence that this is already happening inside the companies developing frontier AI models.

## AI is beginning to help build AI

Perhaps the clearest example comes from Anthropic. In June, the company published an analysis titled When AI Builds Itself, examining how Claude is increasingly involved in developing Anthropic’s own AI systems.

Anthropic is careful to emphasize that full recursive self-improvement has not been achieved and may never happen. Even so, the numbers illustrate how quickly the development process is changing.

As of May 2026, Anthropic said more than 80% of the code merged into its codebase was authored by Claude. The company also reported that its typical engineer was merging around eight times as much code per day in the second quarter of 2026 as in 2024, although Anthropic cautioned that lines of code significantly overstate actual productivity gains.

More importantly, AI’s role is extending beyond simply generating code. Anthropic says Claude can already take relatively underspecified engineering problems and determine how to solve them. On well-defined research experiments, the company says its systems can match or outperform skilled human researchers at execution.

That is creating a fundamentally different development cycle. Historically, humans researched AI and then built better AI systems. Increasingly, humans and AI are conducting that research together, with AI performing larger portions of the work required to develop its successors.

The theoretical next stage would be an AI system capable of choosing important research problems, conducting the experiments, interpreting the results and using those discoveries to develop a better version of itself. That complete loop would represent something much closer to genuine recursive self-improvement.

Anthropic says we are not there yet. But the gap between AI-assisted AI development and autonomous AI development has suddenly become one of the most important questions in technology.

## The missing capability may be judgment

Anthropic’s own research identifies a major limitation in current systems: AI is increasingly capable of executing experiments, but it remains much weaker at deciding which experiments are worth conducting.

That distinction separates technical execution from genuine research judgment. A powerful AI agent may be able to receive an objective, write the necessary code, run thousands of experiments, analyze the results and generate a detailed report. A leading scientist does something different: they identify which problems matter, recognize unexpected results, challenge existing assumptions and invent entirely new research directions.

Anthropic says substantial gaps remain when models are required to exercise this kind of goal-setting judgment. In practical terms, that gap may be one of the main barriers separating today’s AI systems from machines capable of autonomously designing their own successors.

That is an important limitation because humans remain deeply embedded in today’s development loop. People choose the objectives, control the computing infrastructure, verify results and ultimately decide whether a new model should be trained or deployed.

## Critics say this still isn’t the singularity

Not everyone working in AI accepts the increasingly dramatic language coming from Silicon Valley. William Tunstall-Pedoe, a co-creator of Amazon Alexa and founder of AI company UnlikelyAI, has argued that today’s systems lack the kind of autonomous innovation that a true singularity would require. He describes the missing capability as “discovery intelligence” — the ability to independently generate genuinely important new ideas and reliably determine which of those ideas are valuable.

Modern language models can generate enormous numbers of possible answers, hypotheses and approaches. That does not necessarily mean they can recognize the scientific breakthrough hidden among thousands of plausible but unimportant ideas.

Tunstall-Pedoe therefore rejects the claim that the singularity has already arrived. His argument is that genuine runaway self-improvement would produce effects across science, technology and society that would be extraordinarily difficult to miss.

Other researchers make a similar distinction. Even when AI systems demonstrate surprising autonomous behavior, that does not necessarily qualify as a singularity if humans continue to set their objectives and retain the ability to stop them. By that stricter definition, humanity clearly has not crossed the threshold yet.

## The definition of “singularity” may be changing

The disagreement may ultimately come down to what the word itself means. The traditional version of the singularity looks something like this:

Human-level AI → autonomous self-improvement → intelligence explosion → superintelligence.

Under that definition, current AI systems have not reached the singularity. They remain dependent on human-defined objectives, infrastructure and oversight. But a different interpretation is emerging among some AI executives. Under this version, the sequence looks more like:

AI assists humans → humans build better AI faster → better AI accelerates AI research → increasing portions of that process become automated.

Viewed that way, the singularity is not necessarily a single event. It is a process in which the feedback loop between AI capability and AI development becomes progressively faster.

Hassabis’ “foothills” metaphor and Altman’s “gentle singularity” both fit this interpretation. The transformation happens incrementally, even as the underlying rate of technological progress accelerates.

That version sounds less dramatic than a machine suddenly becoming conscious. It may also be more realistic.

## The most important feedback loop in technology

Consider what happens if AI makes AI researchers twice as productive. Those researchers can build a better model faster, and the improved model can then make them even more productive. It might automate experiments that previously required weeks or months, allowing researchers to test vastly more ideas and produce another generation of AI sooner.

As the cycle continues, humans could spend progressively less time performing the research itself and more time choosing objectives and validating machine-generated discoveries. If AI eventually becomes capable of reliably choosing valuable research directions as well, one of the most important remaining human bottlenecks could disappear.

Nobody has demonstrated that complete loop. But frontier AI companies are already using artificial intelligence to automate growing portions of their own development processes, while simultaneously researching what could happen if those systems become capable of more autonomous improvement.
